messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Liam is a 19-year-old White American man who works as a counselor, and when he speaks about the illness that nearly killed him, he does so with a flatness that gives way abruptly to panic when the details come too close. Last year he was hospitalized after a sudden, severe medical crisis that required repeated blood draws, IV lines, and urgent procedures. He remembers the glare of hospital lights on metal trays, the sight of needles being opened, the clear drip chamber hanging beside his bed, and the sharp antiseptic smell that seemed to cling to everything. What has stayed with him is not only fear of dying, but the helplessness of watching his own body fail while strangers moved quickly around him, touching him, inserting lines, examining him, telling him to hold still while he felt less and less certain that his body would keep him alive.

In the months afterward, those reminders kept breaking into ordinary life. Passing the health office at work and catching the sterile smell of disinfectant could make his chest tighten before he had fully registered why. If a client mentioned a medical procedure, or if he saw a syringe in a training video, he felt his body react immediately, with a rush of heat, tension, and the sense that something dangerous was happening now. Medical examinations became especially difficult. Even the idea of being checked by a doctor made him brace as if he were about to be pinned down again. Unexpected movement nearby could set him off in a similar way; if someone reached quickly across a table, he jerked and turned before he could think, already in a state of alarm.

Those moments also began to shape what he believed about himself. Each time he saw a needle or smelled something hospital-like and felt his body surge into panic, Liam took it as proof that his body was still unsafe and fundamentally unreliable. He had come to believe that he could no longer trust his body to tell the difference between danger and safety. What frightened him most was the sense that his body had become an enemy, reacting on its own, dragging him back into terror even in harmless situations. That belief spread beyond the reminders themselves. He described feeling that nothing in his life carried much meaning anymore; the future felt thin and insubstantial compared with how abruptly illness had shown him that his body could fail without warning.

Because of that, he began organizing his life around not setting anything off. At work as a counselor, he quietly traded away tasks that might bring him near health screenings or medical paperwork. If he heard an ambulance outside the building, he waited before stepping into the hallway. He postponed routine physical care and avoided hospitals altogether unless there was no choice. Even in therapy, when discussion started to move toward the hospitalization, he noticed himself shutting it down internally afterward, refusing to think about what had been said once he left the session. He told himself there was no point in opening it up if his body would only ambush him again, and his conviction that his body could not be trusted made avoidance feel like common sense rather than fear.

Sleep became another battleground. Liam started staying up very late most nights, scrolling or watching videos until exhaustion overtook him. In his mind, going to sleep meant letting down his guard; the quiet and stillness gave too much room for the hospital images, the smell, the sense of lying trapped under medical care. The later he stayed up, the more keyed up and physically reactive he felt, and the less rested he was the next day. That constant strain left him even more jumpy, so small movements nearby startled him more easily, and ordinary medical cues hit him with greater force. In that exhausted state, a glimpse of an IV pole in a clinic doorway or the antiseptic scent from a cleaned room could feel almost indistinguishable from being back in the hospital.

As the months passed, the pattern tightened. The more intensely his body reacted, the more certain he became that something in him remained damaged and unsafe, and the more carefully he tried to avoid anything medical, including what came up in therapy. That narrowing of his world made the reminders feel more potent rather than less. A routine examination seemed unbearable precisely because he had stayed away so long. The smell of antiseptic did not register as a neutral odor; it had become a signal that his body was about to betray him again. Even at work, where he is supposed to help others sit with distress, he found himself counting exits, noticing who moved suddenly, and dreading any conversation that veered toward illness.

He finally sought help more urgently after realizing that his life was shrinking around these fears. His girlfriend had started pointing out how often he avoided basic care and how little of himself felt present anymore. Liam was shaken by how hollow he sounded when he said that nothing felt meaningful and by how reflexively he still treated his own body as an adversary. What he is most afraid of is that this reaction means he will never feel safe inside himself again. What he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is to be able to walk into a medical setting, smell the antiseptic air, and not feel as if he is back in the moment when he thought he might die.
